newsitem.title: TAIWAN: INTERVIEW-Taiwan tries bond ratings to spur market.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Taiwan tries bond ratings to spur market.

text.p: Keen to marshal its huge wealth into an Asian-Pacific capital resource, Taiwan on Thursday launches its first ratings company in an ambitious bid to open up and develop its bond and bill markets.
"This will be a big step forward toward Taiwan's financial liberalisation and internationalisation," Chen Chung-hsing, president of the new Taiwan Ratings Corp, told Reuters.

Taiwan Ratings, half-owned by Standard & Poor's, aims to tap S&P ratings know-how to offer high-quality assessments of Taiwan's banks, insurance companies, securities brokerages and listed firms, Chen said in an interview.

Capitalised at T$200 million (US$7.2 million), the firm has blue-ribbon local partners as well -- chiefly the main Taiwan Stock Exchange, the fledgling Over-The-Counter Exchange and the Institute of Securities Futures Markets Development, along with three related institutions.
Chen said the firm aimed to bolster market transparency.
"The establishment of our own ratings system will let investors know clearly bond or bill issuers' debt-payment capability, thus encouraging their holding willingness on bonds and bills," he said.
"Firms with better financial structures that can get higher ratings can issue bonds or bills with lower yields, reducing their issuance costs and thereby boosting such issuance."
Taiwan Ratings' staff of 20 analysts will include two experienced foreign experts.
Chen hopes quality ratings will reduce foreign funds' reluctance to hold Taiwan corporate bonds.
"The ratings system will...attract foreign companies to issue bonds here, helping reach the government goal of becoming an Asia-Pacific funding centre," Chen said.
Taiwan dreams of fashioning itself into a one-stop regional financial centre, with a funding centre as a first step.
Chen said Taiwan urgently needs a ratings system to help it establish financial order as the financial system liberalises, now that the credit market was reaching eye-popping levels.
In 1996, Taiwan firms issued T$6.72 trillion (US$242 billion) in commercial paper, compared with T$442 billion issued 10 years earlier in 1986.
Trading volume has soared too. In 1996, turnover of commercial paper hit T$30 trillion, against T$2.17 trillion in 1986.
"With such a growth rate, we can expect the (annual) domestic short-term capital market scale to exceed T$300 trillion in another 10 years," Chen said.
"With such huge liquidity it's hard to know issuers' credit quality. The need for a ratings agency is urgent," he said.
In 1996, Taiwan firms issued 95 domestic corporate bonds worth T$108.3 billion, up sharply from 28 issues worth T$41.79 billion in 1995.

In 1996, Taiwan firms issued 17 convertible bonds worth T$15.99 billion, up from 16 issues at T$6.95 billion in 1995. In 1996, Taiwan firms issued 15 overseas corporate bonds worth US$1.238 billion, more than triple the US$370 million in 1995.
Chen said Taiwan Ratings would not rate government bonds, saying that as a local agency it was inappropriate to conduct country risk evaluation on the host government.
The first years would focus on educating the market about the benefits of ratings, Chen said. "We don't expect to earn money in the first two years," he said. (US$ = T$27.8)
